title: India Approves Its First Dengue Vaccine as QDENGA Gets DCGI Clearance
excerpt: Takeda's two-dose QDENGA vaccine, approved for ages 4 to 60, marks a turning point in India's fight against a disease that infects hundreds of thousands every year.
body:
• India's drug regulator has approved QDENGA (TAK-003), the country's first-ever dengue vaccine, for individuals aged 4 to 60.
  • Developed by Japan's Takeda, QDENGA is a two-dose vaccine given three months apart and does not require prior dengue infection testing.
  • The vaccine is approved in 41 countries, with nearly 25 million doses distributed globally since 2022.
  • Hyderabad-based Biological E will manufacture QDENGA locally, targeting 50 million doses per year.
  • The full course is estimated at ₹6,000–₹12,000, raising affordability questions for mass deployment.

India on Monday approved its first dengue vaccine after Takeda Pharmaceutical's QDENGA received clearance from the Drugs Controller General of India (DCGI), the company's Indian unit confirmed. The approval makes India the 42nd country to clear the tetravalent vaccine, which targets all four serotypes of the dengue virus.

The Subject Expert Committee (SEC) under the Central Drugs Standard Control Organisation recommended QDENGA for import and distribution for ages 4 to 60, according to Reuters. Takeda must conduct a post-marketing safety and effectiveness study within six months of the vaccine's introduction.

What Is QDENGA and How Does It Work?

QDENGA (TAK-003) is a live-attenuated tetravalent vaccine built on a weakened DENV-2 backbone. Unlike Sanofi's earlier Dengvaxia — which required proof of prior dengue exposure — QDENGA needs no pre-vaccination testing, making large-scale rollout far simpler.

The vaccine is administered as two subcutaneous doses three months apart. In global Phase 3 trials involving more than 28,000 participants across eight countries, Takeda reported roughly 84% efficacy against severe dengue requiring hospitalisation, regardless of prior infection status.

"The vaccine is "disease-modifying," not "transmission-blocking": it reduces severity and hospitalisation but does not prevent infection or end outbreaks."

QDENGA is WHO-prequalified and recommended for children aged 6 to 16 in high-burden areas. The European Medicines Agency extends eligibility to ages 4 through 60 — the range India adopted. Indonesia first approved QDENGA in 2022; Brazil has since added it to its national immunisation programme.

Efficacy Limits and the Serotype Challenge

QDENGA is highly effective against DENV-2 but notably weaker against DENV-3 and DENV-4, especially in seronegative individuals who have never had dengue. That matters because DENV-3 now accounts for 20–30% of cases in several Indian regions and is rising, according to the Observer Research Foundation.

Efficacy also wanes — from about 80% against symptomatic dengue one year after the second dose to roughly 45% by year three, per Lancet data. The vaccine is "disease-modifying," not "transmission-blocking": it reduces severity and hospitalisation but does not prevent infection or end outbreaks. Vector control — fogging, eliminating standing water, community surveillance — remains essential.

Pricing, Access, and Local Manufacturing

Takeda has partnered with Hyderabad-based Biological E to manufacture QDENGA domestically. Biological E targets 50 million doses annually, with a longer-term goal of 100 million per year.

The estimated ₹6,000–₹12,000 cost for two doses poses a barrier. Mass public-sector deployment will likely require government subsidies or inclusion in the Universal Immunisation Programme. India reported over 120,000 dengue cases in 2025; the true burden is almost certainly higher. Meanwhile, Panacea Biotec and ICMR are running Phase III trials for DengiAll, an indigenous candidate targeting all four serotypes, potentially available by 2027.

What This Means for the Diaspora

For Indians abroad who travel home during monsoon season — when dengue peaks from June through November — QDENGA offers a proactive option beyond mosquito repellent. The vaccine is already available in the UK, Germany, Brazil, and other countries, so NRIs can begin the two-dose course before travel. Those who miss the window abroad may access it in India once commercial distribution begins. The lack of mandatory pre-testing simplifies the process for diaspora communities unsure of their prior exposure status.

What Comes Next

Final pricing, distribution timelines, and public-sector inclusion decisions remain open. The mandatory post-marketing study will generate India-specific data — critical given the country's unique serotype mix and population scale. India accounts for roughly a third of the global dengue burden. With monsoon season underway and cases climbing through September, whether QDENGA can move from approval to arms fast enough to matter this year depends on how quickly Biological E, Takeda, and the health ministry align on logistics and public messaging.
